extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy / constitutional theory
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-length exposition of Hobbesian criteria for forms of government, the right and modes of succession, types of dominion (paternal and despotical), and the meaning and limits of subjects' liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three kinds of sovereignty
rubrics_metrics.description: Sovereignty exists in three fundamental forms: Monarchy (one man), Democracy (the general assembly of subjects), and Aristocracy (an assembly of certain persons distinguished from the rest).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Variants that mix features (elective kings, limited kings, provinces governed by representatives of another commonwealth) are to be classified according to who actually holds sovereign power: if an assembly or other body really possesses the right to give or limit power, the government is democratic or aristocratic rather than monarchic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule for appointment of a tutor for an infant sovereign
rubrics_metrics.description: If the preceding monarch has not expressly appointed a tutor, the law of nature provides that tuition shall be in him who by nature has most interest in preserving the infant's authority and to whom least benefit can accrue by the infant's death or diminution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justification: to avoid placing the infant under those who would profit by his destruction. Anti-pattern: leaving an infant in the power of those who can promote themselves by his destruction is described as 'not Tuition, but Trechery.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Assemblies analogous to infants in decision-making
rubrics_metrics.description: Large sovereign assemblies lack the liberty to dissent from the counsel of the majority and in great dangers require temporary dictators or 'Custodes Libertatis' to whom they commit the exercise of power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning: such temporary dictators often fail to return power and may end up deprived of authority as commonly as infant kings are by their protectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elective and limited kings are not necessarily sovereign
rubrics_metrics.description: If a king's power is elective or limited, he is not sovereign in propriety but a minister of the sovereign power that elects or limits him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an elective king can appoint his successor (or otherwise ensure succession), he effectively becomes hereditary/sovereign; if he cannot and no power exists to appoint after his death, the commonwealth dissolves into war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign right to dispose of succession
rubrics_metrics.description: In monarchy the disposing of the succession is always left to the judgment and will of the present possessor (the sovereign), because otherwise the commonwealth would be left without a representative and devolve to war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modes of determining the successor include express words/testament, tacit signs such as custom, or presumption of natural affection when no explicit token exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Succession by express words or testament
rubrics_metrics.description: Succession passes by express words or testament when the monarch declares in life (viva voce or in writing) who shall be his heir; such declaration invests that person immediately after the predecessor's death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Roman emperors declaring their heirs. Note: 'heir' does not imply children only but anyone so declared.

rubrics_metrics.name: Succession by customary acquiescence ('not controlling a custome')
rubrics_metrics.description: Where no testament exists, customary practice is a natural sign of the will: if a custom prescribes that next of kin or male kin succeed, and the possessor did not contradict it in life, that custom provides the right of succession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: whatever custom a man could have controlled but does not control is taken as his tacit will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Succession by presumption of natural affection
rubrics_metrics.description: Absent testament or custom, it is presumed the monarch would prefer his own children (male or female), males over females, nearer kin over remote, and thus succession follows nearest kin in blood and presumed affection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Underlying assumption: parents are more inclined to advance their children and nearer kin confer greater reflected honor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lawfulness of disposing succession to a foreigner
rubrics_metrics.description: It is lawful for a monarch to dispose of the succession by contract or testament even to a stranger/foreigner; inconveniences may follow, but they do not make the disposal unlawful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example/mitigation: Romans integrated conquered peoples into privileges and offices to avoid oppression; marriage with foreigners can similarly bring succession to strangers. Inconvenience arises from unskilful governors, not from the act's illegality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and origin of paternal dominion
rubrics_metrics.description: Paternal dominion (dominion by generation) is the right a parent has over a child, but not because they begat the child — rather because of the child's consent declared expressly or by sufficient signs; in nature, dominion may be disposed by contract or follow from who nourishes or educates the child.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no contract, dominion tends to the mother (first nourisher) or to him who preserves the child; precedent subjection of one parent to another also affects the child's subjection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity of paternal dominion
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever has dominion over a child has dominion over the child's children; dominion over a person's person implies dominion over their possessions and descendants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous to succession rules for monarchy — the right of succession to paternal dominion follows similar rules as for monarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Despotical dominion acquired by consent after conquest
rubrics_metrics.description: Dominion by conquest (despotical) is acquired when the vanquished, to avoid death or bondage, covenant by express words or sufficient signs to grant the victor the use of their life and liberty; conquest alone does not create duty without the vanquished's covenant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinction: captives kept in prison without liberty are not servants and retain a right to break free; only when corporal liberty is allowed and a promise not to flee or revolt is given does servitude arise. 'Quarter' defers death but does not of itself bind the victor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights of a master over a servant in despotical dominion
rubrics_metrics.description: The master of a servant is master of all the servant has and may exact use of goods, labour, servants, and children as often as he thinks fit; the servant holds life by covenant of obedience and cannot accuse the master for injuries resulting from the master's lawful exercise of authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequent to the covenant; if the master punishes or kills for disobedience, the master is author of the action and not accused by the servant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family as a 'little monarchy' but not a commonwealth
rubrics_metrics.description: A family (man with children and/or servants) is in rights of sovereignty like a little monarchy where the father/master is sovereign; but a family is not a commonwealth unless powerful enough to be un-subdueable without hazard of war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a small group is manifestly too weak to defend itself united, individuals may lawfully protect themselves by flight or submission; a family lacks full commonwealth status unless it can resist external force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scriptural justification for absolute sovereign power
rubrics_metrics.description: Scripture passages (e.g., Exodus, Samuel, 1 Kings, Paul's epistles, Jesus' actions) are cited to show that sovereign power has rights to militia, judicature, legislation, and can command for necessary uses; subjects consent to such power (e.g., Israel asking for a king).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: Samuel on the king's rights to take sons/daughters/fields; David restraining servants from killing Saul; 'Give to Caesar' as acknowledgement of sovereign prerogative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign power ought to be absolute
rubrics_metrics.description: For peace and prevention of perpetual war (every man against every man), sovereign power in any commonwealth should be as great as possible; attempts to lessen it subject one to a greater power and risk dissolution into war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objection from practice (where has such power been acknowledged) is rebutted by pointing to the absence of long-lived kingdoms free from sedition or civil war unless subjects never disputed sovereign power. Skill in making and maintaining commonwealths requires rules, not mere practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of liberty (proper sense)
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberty (freedome) properly signifies the absence of external opposition (external impediments of motion); a free-man is one who in things he can do by strength and wit is not hindered from doing what he wills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liberty applies literally to bodies and movement; when applied metaphorically (e.g., free way, free gift) it denotes freedom of those who use it. Distinguishes liberty from power: lack of power due to constitution (sickness, stone stillness) is not lack of liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fear and liberty compatible
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions done from fear (e.g., throwing goods to save a sinking ship) can nonetheless be voluntary; fear does not eliminate liberty if the person could have refused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: paying a debt for fear of imprisonment — action still of a man at liberty because no external force physically prevented omission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty and necessity compatible
rubrics_metrics.description: Voluntary actions proceed from a man's will (liberty) yet also have causes in a chain leading back to God (necessity); seeing the causal connections makes apparent the necessity of voluntary actions without destroying liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: water's liberty to flow and the necessity of its channel. Theological point: God's will assures the necessity of human will while preserving human liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil laws as artificial chains
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil laws are 'artificiall Chains' — bonds fastened by mutual covenants between subjects and sovereign; these bonds may be weak by nature but are held by the danger of breaking them (i.e., enforcement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liberty of subjects is to be understood relative to these covenants: subjects retain liberty in matters the sovereign has left unregulated (buying/selling, choosing abode, trade, instituting children, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject's liberty limited to what sovereign praetermits
rubrics_metrics.description: The liberty of a subject lies only in those things which the sovereign has praetermitted in regulating actions — e.g., liberty to contract, choose abode, trade, institute children — not an exemption from sovereign's power of life and death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies that subjects' demands for absolute exemption from laws or sovereign actions are absurd because lawlessness would make others masters of their lives; true liberty is the freedom left by the sovereign's omissions.
